16	quirks:
17	  - "⛔⛔ THE FIRST ACCOUNT TO REGISTER BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND REGISTRATION IS OPEN, WITH NO CAPTCHA AND NO E-MAIL VERIFICATION. Verified in inventory/user.go:409-413: the user whose row id is 1 is elevated into group 1, the admin group. Nothing seeds an admin: [REDACTED:value] creates settings, a storage policy, three groups, a master node and two OAuth clients, and no user. ⚠️ IGNORE EVERY TUTORIAL THAT TELLS YOU TO READ AN INITIAL PASSWORD OUT OF THE LOG. Cloudreve 3.x printed one; 4.x does not, and there is no CLI to create a user either, so there is nothing to close this window with at deploy time. It is closed only by claiming the account. Register yourself the moment the container answers, before you hand the URL to anyone, and confirm the e-mail address with the user first."
18	  - "⛔ THEN CLOSE REGISTRATION IMMEDIATELY, BECAUSE THE SECOND PROBLEM IS WORSE THAN THE FIRST. inventory/setting.go:499,518,520 ship register_enabled=1, reg_captcha=0, login_captcha=0 and email_active=0, so once you have claimed the admin account ANY stranger can still create their own, instantly and unverified, and [REDACTED:value]:195 gives every new signup 1 GB of storage. On a public hostname that is an open file host with your name on the abuse report. Turn registration off in the admin settings as part of the deploy, not later. Setting CR_SETTING_DEFAULT_register_enabled=0 at deploy time does NOT work as a shortcut here: it would also block YOUR signup, and since there is no CLI to create a user you would have no way in at all."
19	  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH: GET /api/v4/site/ping, which returns a version; GET /api/v4/site/config/<section>, which returns the public site configuration; the login and password-reset endpoints; and any share link that has been created. Files and folders are behind a session. Anonymous browsing of the file tree is not a thing. That is a defensible posture on a public hostname once registration is closed, and an indefensible one before it."
20	  - "⛔ SET CR_CONF_Database.Type=postgres OR IT SILENTLY USES SQLITE. inventory/client.go:52-53 maps an EMPTY database type to sqlite, and client.go:75-78 then opens data/cloudreve.db inside the container. The instance comes up perfectly healthy, serves files, accepts uploads, and loses every account and every file record on the next VM replacement. This is the single easiest way to get this deploy wrong, because upstream's own compose sets the type and a hand-written one usually does not."
21	  - "⛔ SET CR_CONF_Database.Port TOO. It is not optional and its default is not what you expect: pkg/conf/types.go:104-110 defaults Port to 3306, which is MySQL's port. So a compose that sets Type=postgres, Host, User, Password and Name but omits Port will try to reach Postgres on 3306 and fail with a connection error that reads like a network problem."
22	  - "⛔ UPSTREAM'S COMPOSE OMITS THE DATABASE PASSWORD, AND COPYING IT IS THE OTHER WAY THIS BREAKS. Their docker-compose.yml runs its own postgres:17 with POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD=trust, so there is no CR_CONF_Database.Password line to copy. Against redu's managed Postgres you must add one. Full mapping, interpolated in the compose because deploy_compose only APPENDS variables to the project .env and never edits your compose: CR_CONF_Database.Type=postgres, CR_CONF_Database.Host=${PGHOST}, CR_CONF_Database.Port=${PGPORT}, CR_CONF_Database.User=${PGUSER}, CR_CONF_Database.Password=[REDACTED:value]}, CR_CONF_Database.Name=${PGDATABASE}. ONE database, so the managed-Postgres single-database limit that has broken other entries in this library does not apply. No db_superuser is needed: Cloudreve creates TABLES in the database it is given, never a database."
23	  - "PROVE THE DATABASE WIRING IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AFTER BOOT, AND THE LOG GIVES YOU AN EXACT PAIR TO USE. Cloudreve logs which engine it opened (inventory/client.go:77 and :80). Positive half, which also proves your command reached the right container: `sudo docker logs <container> 2>&1 | grep -c 'Connect to Postgres database'` must be at least 1. Negative half: `sudo docker logs <container> 2>&1 | grep -c 'Connect to SQLite database'` must be 0. Belt and braces: `sudo docker exec <container> ls /cloudreve/data/cloudreve.db` must fail with no such file. If the first grep also returns 0, your container name is wrong and the other two results mean nothing. The VM runs docker, not podman."
24	  - "THE CONNECTION TO POSTGRES IS UNENCRYPTED ON THE DEFAULT PATH, DELIBERATELY, AND THE OBVIOUS FIX DOES NOT WORK. inventory/client.go:79-85 builds the DSN from the discrete fields with sslmode=disable HARDCODED, and the Database.SSLMode field declared in pkg/conf/types.go:36 is not consulted there. Over redu's private network between two VMs in the same project that is survivable, and it is worth being deliberate about rather than surprised by. If you do want TLS, use the other code path: set CR_CONF_Database.DatabaseURL to a full connection string with your own sslmode in it (client.go:69-72), and note it then takes precedence over every discrete field."
25	  - "⛔ MOUNT A VOLUME ON /cloudreve/data OR YOU LOSE THE FILES AND THE SESSION SECRET AT THE SAME TIME. This directory is not a cache. It holds the uploaded files themselves, because the default storage policy is local disk; it holds conf.ini, which pkg/conf/conf.go:34-49 generates on first boot with a fresh random SessionSecret that exists NOWHERE ELSE, not in the database; and it holds avatars, thumbnails and the aria2 temp area. Without a volume, a redeploy gives you a database that still lists every file with none of them on disk, plus a new session secret that logs everybody out. The image declares VOLUME /cloudreve/data itself, which creates an ANONYMOUS volume if you do not name one, and an anonymous volume is not something you can rely on finding again."
26	  - "THERE ARE TWO SECRETS, IN TWO DIFFERENT PLACES, AND BOTH HAVE TO SURVIVE. SessionSecret is 64 random characters in conf.ini on the data volume (conf.go:34-49). secret_key is 256 random characters generated at the first migration and stored in the DATABASE settings table (inventory/setting.go:527). Neither is passed in as an environment variable, so there is nothing for you to set, and that is exactly why both are easy to lose: keep the managed Postgres AND the data volume across redeploys and both survive. Lose either one and you have lost half the instance. Do not panic at `HashIDSalt = [REDACTED:value]}` in the generated conf.ini: only the SessionSecret placeholder is substituted, and pkg/conf/types.go:52 marks that field deprecated."
27	  - "⛔ SET CR_SETTING_DEFAULT_siteURL AT DEPLOY TIME, BECAUSE YOU ONLY GET ONE CHANCE. The default is http://localhost:5212 (inventory/setting.go:487) and it is what every share link, e-mail and OAuth redirect is built from. CR_SETTING_DEFAULT_<key> overrides any default setting, but [REDACTED:value]:80-92 applies the override ONLY when the setting does not already exist, so it lands on the FIRST migration and is ignored on every boot afterwards. Get it wrong and the only fix is the admin UI. Generate the dname yourself in the full `cloudreve-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud` form so the https URL is known before you deploy; a bare label gets a random suffix appended by redu and will not match."
28	  - "SET CR_CONF_System.ProxyHeader=X-Forwarded-For. redu terminates TLS at its own proxy, and pkg/conf/types.go:55 shows ProxyHeader defaults to empty, so without it every client IP in the logs, in the ban list and in share access records is redu's proxy rather than the actual visitor."
29	  - "⛔ ARIA2 IS ALWAYS RUNNING IN THIS IMAGE AND YOU CANNOT TURN IT OFF WITH THE OBVIOUS VARIABLE. .build/entrypoint.sh is two lines: it starts supervisord, which starts aria2, and then the server, with no condition on either. The Dockerfile ships CR_ENABLE_ARIA2=1, and [REDACTED:value]:259 reads that variable with os.LookupEnv and IGNORES ITS VALUE, so CR_ENABLE_ARIA2=0 still counts as enabled and still wires the master node to it. What that gives you is remote download: a user with the permission can make YOUR server fetch an arbitrary URL, which on a public host is both a bandwidth-abuse channel and a way to probe addresses only the VM can reach. Control it where it is actually controllable, in the group permissions in the admin UI, and keep registration closed. Related: do NOT publish ports 6888 or 6888/udp, which upstream's compose does and which are aria2's BitTorrent listener. Publish 5212 and nothing else."
30	  - "PORT 5212. The image also exposes 443 and 6888; ignore both. Pass 5212 to deploy_compose. Health probe: GET /api/v4/site/ping, which returns {\"code\":0,\"data\":\"<version>\"} with no authentication. ⚠️ The version in that response is NOT the image tag: routers/controllers/site.go:28-38 returns application/constants/constants.go:6 BackendVersion, which is \"4.14.0\" in the 4.18.0 release because it is the required DB schema version. Do not conclude you pulled the wrong image."
31	  - "PIN cloudreve/cloudreve:4.18.0. Upstream's compose says :latest, and there is also a rolling :v4 tag; neither belongs in a recipe a stranger runs. Their bundled redis:latest and postgres:17 go away entirely with the services they belong to."
32	  - "SERVICES TO DELETE FROM UPSTREAM'S COMPOSE: postgresql (redu provides a managed one on its own private VM, and theirs runs with POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD=trust, meaning no password at all, which is a bad thing to leave running next to a public app). KEEP redis, in the compose and on the app VM, with CR_CONF_Redis.Server=redis:6379: it is the settings cache and the session store, not a system of record, so a redeploy costs everyone a re-login and no data. Cloudreve also runs without Redis at all (pkg/conf/types.go:96-104 defaults the server to empty and it falls back to an in-memory cache), which is a fine choice for a single user."
33	  - "DISK IS THE REAL CONSTRAINT HERE, NOT MEMORY, AND THE USER SHOULD SEE THE NUMBER BEFORE YOU SIZE IT. This is a file store: the default storage policy writes uploads to /cloudreve/data on the app VM. m1.medium comes with 40 GB TOTAL, shared with Ubuntu, docker, and an image that carries libreoffice, ffmpeg, vips and the CJK fonts, so the space actually available for files is meaningfully less than 40 GB. m1.large is 80 GB at GBP 0.0486/hr, and growing either one later is a volume resize rather than a redeploy. Put both numbers in front of the user and let them choose. Third option worth naming: Cloudreve supports S3-compatible remote storage policies, which moves the files off the VM entirely."
34	  - "SET A REAL STORAGE QUOTA ON THE ADMIN GROUP. [REDACTED:value]:163 gives the admin group 1 TB and migration.go:195 gives the default user group 1 GB. Against a 40 GB disk the admin quota is fiction: nothing stops the UI accepting uploads until the filesystem is full, at which point the app and its logs stop being able to write. Set the admin group's quota to something the disk can actually honour."
35	  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO RAM FIGURE, so this file quotes none. The server itself is a single Go binary, which is modest, but the image bundles libreoffice, ffmpeg, vips and libraw and shells out to them for thumbnails and media metadata, and those are bursty and can be large per file. m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB) is the reasoned default and is exactly the no-card trial ceiling, so this entry fits the trial. If thumbnail generation is killing the container, the dials are the CR_SETTING_DEFAULT_thumb_* flags the Dockerfile turns on and the per-generator max-size settings. MEASURE IT on your run and write the figure back."
36	  - "THE IMAGE HARDCODES THE TIMEZONE TO Asia/Shanghai (Dockerfile:5-9), which is upstream's home timezone and is probably not the user's. Every timestamp in the UI and the logs inherits it. Set TZ in the compose to whatever the user wants and say that you did."
37	  - "TWO OAUTH CLIENTS ARE SEEDED WHOSE SECRETS ARE PUBLIC. [REDACTED:value]:277-286 defines the desktop and iOS client GUIDs and secrets as compile-time constants in the public source, and migration.go inserts them into every instance. repo: https://github.com/cloudreve/cloudreve
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: cloudreve/cloudreve:4.18.0
  port: 5212
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: cloudreve
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ THE FIRST ACCOUNT TO REGISTER BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND REGISTRATION IS OPEN, WITH NO CAPTCHA AND NO E-MAIL VERIFICATION. Verified in inventory/user.go:409-413: the user whose row id is 1 is elevated into group 1, the admin group. Nothing seeds an admin: [REDACTED:value] creates settings, a storage policy, three groups, a master node and two OAuth clients, and no user. ⚠️ IGNORE EVERY TUTORIAL THAT TELLS YOU TO READ AN INITIAL PASSWORD OUT OF THE LOG. Cloudreve 3.x printed one; 4.x does not, and there is no CLI to create a user either, so there is nothing to close this window with at deploy time. It is closed only by claiming the account. Register yourself the moment the container answers, before you hand the URL to anyone, and confirm the e-mail address with the user first."
  - "⛔ THEN CLOSE REGISTRATION IMMEDIATELY, BECAUSE THE SECOND PROBLEM IS WORSE THAN THE FIRST. inventory/setting.go:499,518,520 ship register_enabled=1, reg_captcha=0, login_captcha=0 and email_active=0, so once you have claimed the admin account ANY stranger can still create their own, instantly and unverified, and [REDACTED:value]:195 gives every new signup 1 GB of storage. On a public hostname that is an open file host with your name on the abuse report. Turn registration off in the admin settings as part of the deploy, not later. Setting CR_SETTING_DEFAULT_register_enabled=0 at deploy time does NOT work as a shortcut here: it would also block YOUR signup, and since there is no CLI to create a user you would have no way in at all."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH: GET /api/v4/site/ping, which returns a version; GET /api/v4/site/config/<section>, which returns the public site configuration; the login and password-reset endpoints; and any share link that has been created. Files and folders are behind a session. Anonymous browsing of the file tree is not a thing. That is a defensible posture on a public hostname once registration is closed, and an indefensible one before it."
  - "⛔ SET CR_CONF_Database.Type=postgres OR IT SILENTLY USES SQLITE. inventory/client.go:52-53 maps an EMPTY database type to sqlite, and client.go:75-78 then opens data/cloudreve.db inside the container. The instance comes up perfectly healthy, serves files, accepts uploads, and loses every account and every file record on the next VM replacement. This is the single easiest way to get this deploy wrong, because upstream's own compose sets the type and a hand-written one usually does not."
  - "⛔ SET CR_CONF_Database.Port TOO. It is not optional and its default is not what you expect: pkg/conf/types.go:104-110 defaults Port to 3306, which is MySQL's port. So a compose that sets Type=postgres, Host, User, Password and Name but omits Port will try to reach Postgres on 3306 and fail with a connection error that reads like a network problem."
  - "⛔ UPSTREAM'S COMPOSE OMITS THE DATABASE PASSWORD, AND COPYING IT IS THE OTHER WAY THIS BREAKS. Their docker-compose.yml runs its own postgres:17 with POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD=trust, so there is no CR_CONF_Database.Password line to copy. Against redu's managed Postgres you must add one. Full mapping, interpolated in the compose because deploy_compose only APPENDS variables to the project .env and never edits your compose: CR_CONF_Database.Type=postgres, CR_CONF_Database.Host=${PGHOST}, CR_CONF_Database.Port=${PGPORT}, CR_CONF_Database.User=${PGUSER}, CR_CONF_Database.Password=[REDACTED:value]}, CR_CONF_Database.Name=${PGDATABASE}. ONE database, so the managed-Postgres single-database limit that has broken other entries in this library does not apply. No db_superuser is needed: Cloudreve creates TABLES in the database it is given, never a database."
  - "PROVE THE DATABASE WIRING IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AFTER BOOT, AND THE LOG GIVES YOU AN EXACT PAIR TO USE. Cloudreve logs which engine it opened (inventory/client.go:77 and :80). Positive half, which also proves your command reached the right container: `sudo docker logs <container> 2>&1 | grep -c 'Connect to Postgres database'` must be at least 1. Negative half: `sudo docker logs <container> 2>&1 | grep -c 'Connect to SQLite database'` must be 0. Belt and braces: `sudo docker exec <container> ls /cloudreve/data/cloudreve.db` must fail with no such file. If the first grep also returns 0, your container name is wrong and the other two results mean nothing. The VM runs docker, not podman."

# Self-host Cloudreve on redu

Your own file store with sharing links, previews and WebDAV: one Go container, a managed Postgres
for the metadata, a persistent volume for the files, and a public HTTPS URL. About GBP 33 a month.

## What this deploys

- **Cloudreve** from the official image, pinned to 4.18.0, on one m1.medium VM, port 5212.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM for accounts, file records and settings.
- A volume on `/cloudreve/data`, which holds the actual files and the instance's session secret.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Cloudreve on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## One decision to make before you deploy

**How much space do you actually need?** This is a file store, and the disk comes with the VM
rather than separately. m1.medium is 40 GB total, shared with the operating system and a large
image; m1.large is 80 GB. Growing it afterwards is a volume resize, not a redeploy, so it is worth
thirty seconds now. If you expect to store a lot, Cloudreve also supports S3-compatible remote
storage, which takes the files off the VM entirely.

## The three that actually break it

**Open registration, and the first person through the door is the administrator.** There is no
seeded admin account and no printed password in Cloudreve 4, whatever older tutorials say: the
account with row id 1 is promoted to admin, and signup is open with no captcha and no e-mail
verification. So the recipe registers your account the moment the container answers, and then
turns registration off. Leaving it on is an open file host with your name on the abuse report.

**No database type means SQLite.** Cloudreve maps an empty database type to SQLite and writes a
file inside the container. It comes up healthy, serves files, accepts uploads, and loses all of it
on the next redeploy.

**The volume is not optional.** `/cloudreve/data` holds the uploaded files themselves and the
session secret, which exists nowhere else. Wire the database perfectly and skip the volume and you
get a database that lists every file, with none of them on disk.

## After the deploy: prove registration is actually closed

The interesting check is the last one, and note how it works: it POSTs a deliberately incomplete
body to the registration endpoint and reads the application error code rather than the HTTP status,
which are different things here. Cloudreve answers HTTP 200 either way. A closed instance rejects
the request before it ever looks at the body, so the two cases are distinguishable **without ever
creating an account**.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cloudreve post-deploy check. Usage: check.sh cloudreve-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# exit 0 = healthy and locked down, 1 = FAIL (act now), 2 = usage, 3 = inconclusive
set -u
HOST="$1"
[ -n "$HOST" ] || { echo "usage: check.sh cloudreve-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud" >&2; exit 2; }

BODY=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$BODY"' EXIT

# POSITIVE CONTROL FIRST. Nothing below means anything unless we are really talking to Cloudreve.
code=$(curl -sS -o "$BODY" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/v4/site/ping")
if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from the edge, the container is still starting. Re-run in a minute."
  exit 3
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/v4/site/ping answered $code, not 200."
  exit 3
fi
if ! grep -q '"code":0' "$BODY"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: ping was 200 but did not carry the Cloudreve success envelope."
  exit 3
fi
echo "OK: Cloudreve is answering (the version it reports is the DB schema version, not the tag)"

# THE ONE THAT MATTERS. Probe the registration endpoint with a body that can never succeed: no
# password field at all. Registration DISABLED is refused by middleware BEFORE the body is read,
# and answers code 40019. Registration ENABLED gets as far as validating the body, and answers
# code 40001. Neither creates an account. Bodies go on stdin, never in argv.
printf '%s' '{"email":"probe@example.invalid"}' \
  | curl -sS -o "$BODY" -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @- \
         "https://$HOST/api/v4/user" >/dev/null

if grep -q '"code":40019' "$BODY"; then
  echo "OK: registration is CLOSED (feature-not-enabled)"
elif grep -q '"code":40001' "$BODY"; then
  echo "FAIL: registration is OPEN. Anyone can create an account on this instance right now."
  echo "If no admin exists yet, the first person to sign up also becomes the administrator."
  exit 1
else
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the registration probe returned neither 40019 nor 40001. Do not assume"
  echo "this instance is safe; open the admin settings and check registration by hand."
  exit 3
fi
```

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cloudreve post-deploy check. Usage: check.sh cloudreve-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# exit 0 = healthy and locked down, 1 = FAIL (act now), 2 = usage, 3 = inconclusive
set -u
HOST="$1"
[ -n "$HOST" ] || { echo "usage: check.sh cloudreve-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud" >&2; exit 2; }

BODY=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$BODY"' EXIT

# POSITIVE CONTROL FIRST. Nothing below means anything unless we are really talking to Cloudreve.
code=$(curl -sS -o "$BODY" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/v4/site/ping")
if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from the edge, the container is still starting. Re-run in a minute."
  exit 3
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/v4/site/ping answered $code, not 200."
  exit 3
fi
if ! grep -q '"code":0' "$BODY"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: ping was 200 but did not carry the Cloudreve success envelope."
  exit 3
fi
echo "OK: Cloudreve is answering (the version it reports is the DB schema version, not the tag)"

# THE ONE THAT MATTERS. Probe the registration endpoint with a body that can never succeed: no
# password field at all. Registration DISABLED is refused by middleware BEFORE the body is read,
# and answers code 40019. Registration ENABLED gets as far as validating the body, and answers
# code 40001. Neither creates an account. Bodies go on stdin, never in argv.
printf '%s' '{"email":"probe@example.invalid"}' \
  | curl -sS -o "$BODY" -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @- \
         "https://$HOST/api/v4/user" >/dev/null

if grep -q '"code":40019' "$BODY"; then
  echo "OK: registration is CLOSED (feature-not-enabled)"
elif grep -q '"code":40001' "$BODY"; then
  echo "FAIL: registration is OPEN. Anyone can create an account on this instance right now."
  echo "If no admin exists yet, the first person to sign up also becomes the administrator."
  exit 1
else
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the registration probe returned neither 40019 nor 40001. Do not assume"
  echo "this instance is safe; open the admin settings and check registration by hand."
  exit 3
fi

Deployed and locked down.

## Your instance

**https://cloudreve-1jjc6hxu.redu.cloud**

- **Login:** `«REDACTED:env:013044ef»`
- **Password:[REDACTED:value] `«REDACTED:entropy:2bbc76d2»`

Change it in the UI and put it in your password manager — it's only in this session and deliberately not in any file on disk.

## What ran

`check_deploy_prerequisites` → `plan_deploy` → your approval → upload-mode `deploy_compose` (deployment #444). m1.medium app VM + m1.small managed Postgres, **GBP 0.0452/hr ≈ GBP 33/mo**, exactly as `redu.md` predicted.

The three failure modes the recipe warns about were all checked, not assumed:
- **Not on SQLite** — `Connect to Postgres database` ×1, `Connect to SQLite database` ×0, and `/cloudreve/data/cloudreve.db` doesn't exist.
- **Volume is real and named** — `app-src_cloudreve_data` mounted at `/cloudreve/data`, holding the `conf.ini` that carries the only copy of the SessionSecret.
- **Registration window closed** — I claimed the admin account ~10 seconds after the container first answered, then set `register_enabled=0`. `check.sh` confirms code 40019 without creating an account.

Also: `siteURL` landed correctly on the first (only) migration, TZ is Europe/Belgrade (the register response timestamped `+02:00`), only 5212 is published — 6888 is not — and I lowered the admin group quota from its fictional 1 TB to 25 GiB.

## Two things worth your attention

**A real bug in the recipe, found by testing rather than trusting a 200.** Setting the admin group's quota via `PUT /api/v4/admin/group/1` — sending back the exact object the GET returned — answers `code 0` and **silently unbinds the group's storage policy**. Uploads then fail with `50001 Failed to get available storage policies`, an error that names storage policies and not the group you just edited. Fixed by passing `edges.storage_policies` instead of the scalar field; I then proved it with a real upload (file written to the named volume on the host, read back byte-identical, deleted). Had I stopped at the 200, you'd have had a file store that couldn't store files.

**A prediction in `redu.md` was wrong.** `/api/v4/site/ping` returns `4.18.0`, not the `4.14.0` the file expected. I corrected that quirk rather than leaving the next reader to trip over it.

## The number the file was waiting for

**34 GB actually free for files** (38 GB filesystem, 4.2 GB eaten by the OS and the two images). Idle RAM was 720 MB of 3915 — so disk is confirmed as the binding constraint, not memory. That makes m1.medium a good default for a personal file store and a poor one for anything archival; m1.large (80 GB) or an S3 policy is the move if you expect volume.

## Files written

`docker-compose.yml`, `check.sh`, `redu-deploy-plan.md` (real provisioned values + measurements), and `redu.md` — updated with `last_deploy`, a `measured:` block, the deploy-log entry, and **five new quirks** covering the group-PUT bug, the non-guessable admin API routes, the end-to-end upload proof, and the measured sizing.

One thing to know before you tear this down: `delete_deployment` removes the app VM, **and on this app the app VM is where your files live**. The managed Postgres survives and keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr, holding metadata for files that would no longer exist. Get your data out first, then delete both.
